hook.en: A corner shop owner writes cash in a notebook and keeps a list of customers who owe him. He has no ledger for sales, rent or furniture. Can we still find his capital and profit?

objectives.en: Explain what incomplete records (single entry) are
List their features, reasons and limitations
Prepare a statement of affairs to find capital

narration.en: A corner shop owner writes cash in a notebook and keeps a list of customers who owe him. He has no ledger for sales, rent or furniture. Can we still find his capital and profit?

body.en: Accounts are called incomplete records when transactions are not recorded fully on the double entry system. Usually only a cash book and the personal accounts of debtors and creditors are kept, while real and nominal accounts are missing. This practice is sometimes loosely called the single entry system. It is common among small traders, who find full double entry costly or unnecessary.

points.en: Usually only cash and personal accounts are kept
Nominal and real accounts are often missing
A trial balance cannot be prepared, so arithmetic accuracy is not proved
Different traders follow different methods: there is no uniformity

title.en: Reasons, limitations and the statement of affairs

body.en: Incomplete records are simple and cheap, but they cannot show the true profit or financial position, errors and frauds are hard to detect, and tax authorities and banks may not accept them. To find capital on a date, an accountant prepares a statement of affairs: a list of assets and liabilities, with capital as the excess of assets over liabilities. Unlike a balance sheet, it is built from estimates and partial records.

points.en: Statement of affairs: based partly on estimates
Balance sheet: based on ledger balances of a double entry system
A deficiency arises when liabilities exceed assets
